01.r: Turns from the slaves to the king's enemies.
01.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'yet, howbeit, only' when it introduces a clause, and says it is used like ἀλλά and δέ.

02.r: Marks the particular enemies already spoken of in the parable.

03.r: The citizens who opposed the nobleman becoming king.
03.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from ἔχθος, hatred; actively it means 'hating, hostile'.

05.r: Points to the enemies as present to the speaker's mind.

06.r: The article turns the phrase that follows into a description of the enemies.

07.n: This is the negative Abbott-Smith calls subjective, used where the negation depends on a condition or on what one thinks; it is the usual negative with a participle.

08.r: Their will was set against his rule.
08.n: An aorist participle: their refusal is looked at as one settled act. Abbott-Smith gives 'to will, be willing, wish, desire'.

10.r: To have royal power over them.
10.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to be king, to reign, rule', and lists this verse among those where ἐπί, 'over', follows, which he likens to the Hebrew idiom.

13.r: An order to his attendants to bring the enemies in.
13.n: An aorist imperative, plural: a command to those standing by.

14.n: Abbott-Smith notes that in late writers the word is used of place, both 'hither' and 'here'.

16.r: Put them to death, all of them.
16.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to kill off, slay', and this is its only New Testament occurrence. The prefix κατα- adds completeness, which 'kill off' and our 'slaughter' try to keep.

18.n: Abbott-Smith's sense as a preposition is 'before', and first 'in front of'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads ἐκείνους, 'those', where our text has τούτους, 'these', and it lacks the second αὐτούς, 'them'. The KJV's 'those mine enemies' follows the first reading; its 'slay them' supplies the pronoun in English, while the YLT's 'slay before me' matches the shorter Greek.
